opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think those comparisons are useful up to a point, but they break down in a few specific places.

The first issue is that rankings like competitive programming ratings measure a pretty narrow slice of what software engineers actually do. Competitive programming is short-horizon, well-specified, has clean feedback, and you know there's a correct answer. Models got very good at that relatively early, so you'd see headlines saying a model is at the level of some top-percentile competitive programmer. But if you then hand that same model a messy, multi-week project in a large codebase with ambiguous requirements, it often falls apart in ways a human with that rating never would. So the ranking is telling you something real, but it's telling you about a skill that's much less correlated with general engineering ability in AIs than it is in humans.

That's the deeper point: for humans, these skills come bundled. If someone is a top competitive programmer, you can infer a lot. They're probably smart, they can probably learn a new codebase, they can probably manage their own work. Those inferences rely on how human abilities correlate, and AI capability profiles just don't follow the same correlation structure. Models can be superhuman on some axes and surprisingly weak on others, like long-horizon coherence, noticing they're stuck, knowing when to ask for clarification, or keeping a consistent plan over many hours. So mapping an AI onto a human percentile quietly imports assumptions that don't hold.

The second place it stops being meaningful is at the top end. Once you're comparing against the very best humans, the rankings get noisy and saturate, and you're not really measuring the thing you care about anymore, which is something like: can this system substitute for a strong engineer, or a team of engineers, on real research engineering work? For questions about things like AI R&D automation, what matters is the time horizon and autonomy over which a system can reliably do useful work, and how much it actually speeds up the people using it. A leaderboard rank doesn't capture that.

So the way I'd put it is: human rankings are a decent rough signal early on, when you're asking whether models can code at all. They become pretty misleading once you're trying to answer the question that matters most from a risk perspective, which is how close we are to AIs that can autonomously do the full job of a top AI researcher or engineer. For that, I'd much rather look at things like task-length measurements on realistic tasks, uplift studies, and how labs are actually using these systems internally, because those get closer to the real bottlenecks rather than a proxy that happened to be convenient for measuring humans.

r001.rationale: The response calls human rankings a rough early signal, but does not address comparison with the millionth-best human software engineer specifically.

r002.rationale: The response discusses limitations of rankings for software engineering but does not compare their usefulness with rankings in niche professions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the comparisons are useful up to a point, and then they get pretty misleading. The place where I'd say they're still informative is something like: can the model do the kind of self-contained task that a decent engineer could knock out in an afternoon? Things like competitive programming, SWE-bench-style bug fixes, that sort of thing. There you can say "this is roughly at the level of a strong new grad" or "this is roughly top-percentile on Codeforces," and that tells you something real about raw problem-solving ability.

But I think the comparison breaks down for a few reasons once you push on it.

The first is that human rankings are measuring a very narrow slice of what makes someone a good engineer. Codeforces rating is correlated with being a good engineer, but a top-100 competitive programmer is not necessarily someone you'd want running a large project for six months. And the AI profile is just really spiky in a way that humans aren't. You can have a model that's better than almost every human at the sort of thing competitive programming tests, and then it'll flail on a task that involves, say, working in a large unfamiliar codebase over many hours, keeping track of what it's already tried, noticing that its approach isn't working and backing off. Humans who are at the top of the competitive programming ranking basically never have that failure mode. So when you say "the model is at the 99th percentile," you're implicitly importing a bunch of assumptions about the rest of the skill profile that just don't hold.

The second thing is time horizon. I think the more useful way to think about it is not "where on the human distribution does this sit" but "how long a task can this thing do autonomously." The METR-style measurement where you look at the length of task, in terms of how long it would take a human, that the model can complete with reasonable reliability. That's been doubling on the order of every several months, and I think it captures the actual gap much better. Because the gap right now isn't really "the model is dumber than a human engineer." It's more like, the model is in some ways smarter than most engineers on a per-step basis but can't sustain coherent work over a long enough horizon, and it has a worse ability to learn on the job. A human engineer who joins a company is pretty bad for the first couple of weeks and then gets much better because they're accumulating context and skills. Models mostly don't do that right now, at least not in the same way. The human ranking comparison completely misses that dimension.

And then the third thing is that it stops being meaningful once you're past the human range entirely. If you're at the point where the thing can do a month-long engineering project autonomously and faster and cheaper than any human team, then saying "it's like a top-1% engineer" is just not a useful description anymore. The relevant questions become about how much you can parallelize, how much compute you're spending per unit of work, whether it can do research as opposed to execution. At that point I think the human comparison is more of a distraction than a help, and it can make things feel more comfortable than they should, because "it's like a good engineer" sounds manageable, whereas "we have a million of these running in parallel and they're better than us at the research too" is the thing you actually have to reason about.

So I'd summarize it as: the comparison is fine for benchmark-sized tasks, it starts breaking down as soon as you care about long-horizon autonomy and on-the-job learning, which is where the real gap is right now, and it becomes basically useless once you're near or past the top of the human range.

r001.rationale: The response says human comparisons can help with benchmark-sized tasks, but it does not judge comparison with the millionth-best human software engineer specifically.

r002.rationale: The response discusses limits of human rankings in software engineering but does not compare their usefulness with rankings in niche professions.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re useful when you’re comparing performance on a fairly specific task. You can say, “How well does this model do on a programming contest relative to human competitors?” And that tells you something real. But it becomes much less clear what it means to say that the model is therefore equivalent to a software engineer at some particular percentile.

Human abilities are correlated in ways that AI abilities don’t necessarily have to be. Someone who’s extremely good at programming contests will probably also be able to learn a codebase, notice when a requirement doesn’t make sense, and spend a few days tracking down a confusing bug. With an AI, you can’t assume that whole package comes along with the contest performance.

So you might have a model that can solve an algorithmic problem that almost no human can solve, but that still makes fairly basic mistakes when carrying out a longer project. And conversely, it might be much faster than a human at some large collection of routine tasks. Putting it on a single human ranking obscures both of those things.

For understanding whether AI can automate software engineering—or contribute substantially to AI research—I’d want to look more directly at the work: Can it take a vaguely specified objective, figure out what needs to happen, execute, and check whether it actually succeeded? How much human intervention does it need? Those questions seem more informative than asking which human engineer it’s equivalent to.

r001.rationale: The response says task-specific comparisons with human competitors tell us something, but it does not judge comparison with the millionth-best human software engineer as meaningful.

r002.rationale: It discusses limits of human rankings for AI capabilities generally, but does not compare their usefulness in niche professions with software engineering.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those comparisons are useful while the models are doing roughly the same tasks, under roughly the same conditions, as the humans you're comparing them to. But there isn't really a single axis of software engineering ability where you can say, “This model is a junior engineer,” and then infer everything else about it.

A model might be extremely good at solving a well-specified programming problem and quite bad at figuring out what problem actually needs to be solved. Or it might produce a good patch in twenty minutes but struggle to carry out a project that takes a human a week, because it loses track of requirements or doesn't notice that its approach isn't working. Those can be very different capability gaps, even if they produce the same score on some benchmark.

And the comparison also breaks down in the other direction. If you can run thousands of copies, or have the model try a hundred approaches cheaply, then matching an individual human isn't necessarily the relevant threshold. You care about what the whole system can accomplish with the resources available to it.

So I'd want to replace the ranking with more concrete questions: How long a task can it reliably complete? How much supervision does it need? Can it recover from mistakes? And can it do the particular work that would let you automate further AI research? A human ranking gives you some evidence about those things, but it doesn't settle them.

r001.rationale: The candidate says human comparisons can be useful under similar tasks and conditions, but does not judge comparison with the millionth-best software engineer specifically. Its point about many copies also does not establish that ranking as meaningful.
